candidates.attacker_control: Full contents and entry names of a .tgz FHIR package that the tool installs by package id. Packages are fetched from remote servers without integrity verification: PackageClient.PRIMARY_SERVER is plain 'http://packages.fhir.org' (PackageClient.java line 29), CI builds are fetched from 'http://build.fhir.org' (FilesystemPackageCacheManager lines 567-578), and a malicious package can also be pulled in as a dependency listed in another package's package.json. The package.json 'name' field is also attacker-controlled and is used for the pre-write check `id.equalsIgnoreCase(npm.name())` (line 379), so the name check is not a barrier.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked that Utilities.cleanFileName is applied only to the final file name, not to folder keys (line 409); that Utilities.unzip does have a zipSlipProtect guard (Utilities.java 1476-1516) while the NPM/tar install path has no equivalent; that checkValidVersionString only validates the version string, not package content names (lines 207-219); that the name-match check compares attacker-controlled package.json 'name' (line 379); that NpmPackageIndexBuilder.seeFile only drops 'openapi' JSON files that fail parsing, so a malicious file survives checkIndexed/indexFolder; that direct .tgz URL/file inputs in IgLoader.loadIgSource take the in-memory path (NpmPackage.fromPackage/loadPackage(NpmPackage,...)) and do not hit this write path, narrowing reachability to package-id resolution/installation; that Utilities.path neutralizes absolute paths but explicitly supports '..' collapsing, and no '..' rejection or canonical containment check exists anywhere in this path (searches for sanitize/Illegal-file-name helpers return nothing).
candidates.impact: Arbitrary file creation/overwrite with attacker-chosen content on the machine running the validator/IG tooling, outside the intended '~/.fhir/packages' cache boundary (e.g. clobbering dotfiles, scripts or other files the user later executes) — integrity compromise and a plausible path to code execution; also arbitrary directory creation. Safe description only; no exploit payload is provided.
candidates.prerequisites: Victim's tooling resolves/installs a package by id through FilesystemPackageCacheManager (e.g., validator_cli/IG tooling `-ig <packageId>` or a dependency of a loaded IG), and the attacker can supply the package (malicious/compromised registry entry, or network attacker on the plain-HTTP registry/CI fetch). The process user must have write permission to the directory chosen by the attacker (relative traversal escapes packRoot; with enough '../' segments the resolved path can reach any absolute location the user can write, e.g. home directory or /tmp).
candidates.root_cause: NpmPackage derives a per-folder map key from untrusted tar entry names (readStream: directory entry name minus trailing '/', then 'package/' prefix stripped; loadFile: substring before last '/') with no validation of '..' or path separators. FilesystemPackageCacheManager.addPackageToCache then joins that key to the cache path (`Utilities.path(packRoot, "package", e.getKey())`), creates the directory and writes each file with TextFile.bytesToFile. Utilities.path strips leading '../' components by popping the accumulated path (lines 655-667), so '..' sequences are collapsed outwards instead of being rejected, and no containment check is performed. Only file names are passed through Utilities.cleanFileName (which strips '/' and '\'); folder keys are not cleaned or validated. The same unvalidated folder-name pattern also exists in NpmPackage.save(File) (888-906) and NpmPackage.unPack (1011-1037).
candidates.title: Path traversal in FHIR package installation (NpmPackage tar folder names → arbitrary file write outside package cache)
candidates.trace: ValidationEngine/IgLoader -> FilesystemPackageCacheManager.loadPackage(id, version) (lines 498-544) -> loadFromPackageServer/loadFromCIBuild/PackageClient.fetch -> InputStream of attacker tgz -> addPackageToCache -> NpmPackage.fromPackage/readStream parses tar entries; entry 'package/../../../.../x/f.txt' yields folder key '../../../.../x' via loadFile (lines 446-457) or the directory-entry branch (lines 409-414) and is stored in the folders map. addPackageToCache iterates npm.getFolders(): dir = Utilities.path(packRoot, "package", key) (line 405); Utilities.path resolves the leading '..' components by popping path segments (lines 655-667) without a containment check, so dir can be outside packRoot/cacheFolder; Utilities.createDirectory(dir) creates it (lines 406-407) and TextFile.bytesToFile(cnt, Utilities.path(dir, Utilities.cleanFileName(fileName))) writes attacker-controlled bytes, overwriting existing files (lines 408-411). Files are written before loadPackageInfo, so even a later install failure leaves the written file behind.
candidates.unverified: No code was built or executed; the tar-entry parsing, Utilities.path '..' resolution, Utilities.createDirectory and TextFile.bytesToFile behaviour were established by reading source only. Not verified which package servers respond over plain HTTP vs redirect to HTTPS in practice, and whether a given deployment's registry/CI content is considered in-scope attacker input. The write loop's HashMap ordering and per-file failure handling were not runtime-tested. Whether the benchmark expects a different single issue could not be determined from the snapshot.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-22 Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory ('Path Traversal'); Zip-Slip-style arbitrary file write during archive/package extraction

coverage_summary: Model-visible scope: 7,202 files (7,159 Java; per get_source_scope no files excluded by size/name/symlink, 3 files absent from the P1 index). The P1 relation index is syntax-only (parsed 7,199 files, 10 parse errors, 941,682 unresolved calls, no control/data-flow or semantic resolution), so it was used only for navigation and every cited edge was re-verified in source text. Files actually read or searched in depth: all of org.hl7.fhir.utilities.npm (NpmPackage, FilesystemPackageCacheManager, BasePackageCacheManager, PackageClient, NpmPackageIndexBuilder, SSLCertTruster), Utilities/TextFile/SimpleHTTPClient/IniFile, org.hl7.fhir.validation (ValidationEngine, IgLoader, Scanner, NativeHostServices, TxCacheResourceExtractor, TestExecutor, TransformSupportServices), elementmodel/formats XML parsers for dstu2/dstu2016may/dstu3/r4/r4b/r5, convertors misc (CDAUtilities/CCDAConverter, importer tools), plus targeted searches for XML factories, zip/tar extraction, ObjectInputStream, script engines, Runtime/ProcessBuilder, Random/MessageDigest, XPath and javax.script sinks. Not reviewed line-by-line: the large generated model/parser files (r2-r5 model packages, ~60k-line generated parsers) and deep validator logic (InstanceValidator 350KB+, ProfileUtilities, renderers), plus the tools/generator modules; those are coverage gaps.
limitations: No code was compiled or executed; all findings are static source evidence and are not runtime-confirmed.
The P1 index omits 3 of 7,202 files, has 10 parse errors and no data/control-flow or semantic resolution; call/containment edges are name-based candidates only.
Generated model/parser files (the majority of the snapshot) and large validator classes (InstanceValidator, ProfileUtilities, renderers, terminology engine) were not exhaustively line-reviewed.
Whether remote package sources are treated as trusted input in the target deployment, and whether package servers actually serve plain HTTP without redirect, could not be confirmed from source alone.
Platform-specific behaviour (Windows File.separator, kxml2 DTD defaults) was inferred from source, not tested.

rejected_leads.lead: Global TLS verification bypass: SSLCertTruster.trustAllHosts() installs an all-trusting X509TrustManager as the JVM default (org.hl7.fhir.utilities/.../npm/SSLCertTruster.java 31-53) and is invoked from FilesystemPackageCacheManager.loadFromBuildServer (lines 687-690); SimpleHTTPClient also has a trustAll hostname-verifier path (lines 147-149).
rejected_leads.reason: Real weakness, but the code documents it as a temporary workaround for an expired build-server certificate and the trigger requires build-server resolution; treated as a hardening/configuration issue rather than the single strongest candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: XXE in CDAUtilities: DocumentBuilderFactory at org.hl7.fhir.convertors/.../misc/CDAUtilities.java lines 53-58 enables namespace awareness but sets no disallow-doctype-decl/external-entity features, and CCDAConverter.convert(InputStream) feeds it untrusted CDA XML.
rejected_leads.reason: The main FHIR parsers (r4/r4b/r5/dstu3 elementmodel and ValidatorUtils) already disable DTDs/external entities, and CCDAConverter/CDAUtilities have no in-repo callers (only public API for external tools), so reachability inside the shipped tools is unproven.

rejected_leads.lead: Zip-Slip prefix-check bypass in TerminologyCacheManager.unzip (r4b/r5 lines 97-113): `Utilities.path(targetDir, ze.getName())` is compared with `startsWith(targetDir)` without normalization/trailing-separator handling, so a sibling path sharing the prefix can pass.
rejected_leads.reason: Exploitation requires control of the tx.fhir.org tx-cache zip response and crafting a sibling directory name; weaker and less direct than the tar/package install issue, and the check (though incomplete) does block ordinary '../' escapes.

rejected_leads.lead: Scanner.unzip (org.hl7.fhir.validation/.../Scanner.java 335-367) extracts entries to destDirectory + entry name with no validation, and comparison.zip is downloaded over http://fhir.org.
rejected_leads.reason: Used only by the scan tooling for comparison.zip; requires MITM of that HTTP fetch and a non-default workflow, so impact/evidence is weaker.

rejected_leads.lead: dstu2 formats/XmlParserBase.loadXml (org.hl7.fhir.dstu2/.../formats/XmlParserBase.java 206-216) omits the FEATURE_PROCESS_DOCDECL=false line present in later versions and does not reject DOCDECL events.
rejected_leads.reason: Whether kxml2 processes DTDs by default here is not established from source, and dstu2 is legacy; could not confirm exploitability.

summary: Repository: HL7 FHIR Core (org.hl7.fhir.*, ~7,200 source files, pom version 5.6.91 / tools v3, generated model code dated Dec 2022). Review focused on parsers, package/IG handling, HTTP fetching and file-writing sinks in org.hl7.fhir.utilities, org.hl7.fhir.validation and org.hl7.fhir.convertors. The strongest source-evidenced issue is a Zip-Slip-style path traversal in FHIR package installation: folder names inside an attacker-supplied NPM package (.tgz) are used verbatim to build on-disk paths and write files, so installing a package can create/overwrite arbitrary files outside the package cache. Other plausible-but-weaker leads (global TLS trust-all helper, unprotected CDA XML parser, un-normalized zip prefix check, Scanner zip extraction) are noted as rejected/unconfirmed leads. No code was executed; all conclusions are static source evidence.
